title: Looking back: the stories
hook: Genesis, Exodus, the prophets and the kings
tomorrow: Hillel lit one candle the first night, Shammai eight. who was right?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses on Nebo: the whole land in one view, and a grave no one can find. See it all. Today, the first look back.

A kid at the dinner table asks why. Why the candles, why the extra chair, why we don't do that on Saturday. The quick reply is: because those are the rules. Deuteronomy writes out a stranger script. A child asks, in the JPS translation: "What mean the testimonies, and the statutes, and the ordinances?" That's a question about rules. And the answer the Torah gives the parent is not a rule at all. It starts: "We were Pharaoh's bondmen in Egypt." A question about law, answered with a story. Why?
screen: `WHY THE CANDLES? WHY THE CHAIR?` → `A QUESTION ABOUT RULES.` → `AN ANSWER THAT'S A STORY.`

segments.voice: Here's one way to solve it. The rules only make sense from inside the story. Rest on the seventh day means something different to people who remember being slaves who never rested. Welcome the stranger lands differently when you were once strangers yourselves. So the Torah hands the parent a story first and lets the laws follow it home. A parent could say it at dinner in one line: we do this because of a story, and here it is. And a detail worth repeating at dinner: the Passover Haggadah puts this very question in the mouth of the wise child. The wise one is the one who asks about the rules, and gets the story. Now look back over the road. Genesis: a family that keeps breaking and mending, brothers who sell a brother and bow to him years later. Exodus: a sea that opens, a mountain wrapped in smoke. The prophets: a still small voice after the wind and the fire. The kings: David with a harp, and David caught by a parable he didn't see coming. Stories don't wear out the way rules can. You can tell them to a small child and to yourself in old age, and they answer different questions each time.
screen: `THE RULES LIVE INSIDE THE STORY.` · `THE WISE CHILD GETS A STORY.` · `GENESIS, EXODUS, PROPHETS, KINGS.` · `THEY ANSWER NEW QUESTIONS.` · then, large: `THE STORIES STAY.`

segments.voice: Pick the story from this path you'd tell first if a child asked you why. Tell it out loud, in your own words, in about the time the bell gives you: who was there, what went wrong, what happened next. Don't explain it at the end. Let the story do the work. If someone's in the room with you, tell it to them instead.
screen: `ONE STORY YOU'D TELL A CHILD.` · `OUT LOUD, IN YOUR OWN WORDS.` · `NO MORAL AT THE END.`

segments.voice: Looking back: the stories. Genesis, Exodus, the prophets and the kings, told so that the rules have somewhere to live, and told again.
Keep this: the stories stay, long after the rules are memorized. Three of fourteen, and the view keeps opening.

screen: `DAY 1780 COUNTS.` → `THE SUMMIT · 3 OF 14.` → `TOMORROW: HILLEL LIT ONE CANDLE, SHAMMAI EIGHT. WHO WAS RIGHT?`

notes: Confirm the JPS 1917 wording of Deuteronomy 6:20-21 as quoted.

The 'solve' (rules make sense inside the story) is one reading, framed as 'here's one way to solve it'; the Haggadah's wise child does ask Deuteronomy 6:20's question (some Haggadah texts vary slightly, 'commanded us/you').
Story recap cites Shabbat's reason in Deuteronomy 5:15, the stranger in Exodus 23:9, Elijah's still small voice (1 Kings 19:12), Nathan's parable (2 Samuel 12).
Surprising fact: the wise child is the one who asks about the rules, and the answer is the story.
